claims.claim: Being and Time is by Martin Heidegger, 1927
claims.evidence: SEP Heidegger intro: "His magnum opus, Being and Time (1927)"

claims.claim: It presents humans as always caught up in a shared world
claims.evidence: SEP Existentialism 2.3: "someone who is always already involved and engaged with the equipment, institutions, and practices of a shared world"

claims.claim: Humans are lost in 'the They'
claims.evidence: SEP Existentialism 5.4: "when I was lost and scattered in 'the They'"

claims.claim: Anxiety calls them back from 'the They'
claims.evidence: SEP Existentialism 5.4: "anxiety as an individualizing mood, one that momentarily 'snatches one back' from the tranquilizing routines of 'the They'" (note: source stresses this is momentary; 'until' slightly implies a lasting return, acceptable at this length)

claims.claim: The Myth of Sisyphus is by Albert Camus, 1942
claims.evidence: SEP Camus 3: "released The Stranger in June 1942 and The Myth of Sisyphus in October"

claims.claim: It asks whether life is worth living
claims.evidence: SEP Camus intro: "There is only one really serious philosophical question, and that is suicide"; SEP Camus 1: "the questions posed by The Myth of Sisyphus, 'Why should I not kill myself?'" (paraphrase preserves meaning)

claims.claim: Its image is Sisyphus pushing his rock up a mountain, again and again, forever
claims.evidence: SEP Camus 1: "Sisyphus straining to push his rock up the mountain, watching it roll down, then descending after the rock to begin all over, in an endless cycle"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Being and Nothingness is by Sartre, 1943
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre 4.1: "Being and Nothingness (1943)"

claims.claim: It is the movement's defining book
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre 4.1: "Being and Nothingness (1943) remains the defining treatise of the existentialist 'movement', along with works from de Beauvoir from this period". The text drops 'along with works from de Beauvoir', making it the sole defining book.

claims.claim: It is on our absolute freedom
claims.evidence: SEP Existentialism 4.2: "In Being and Nothingness, Sartre forwards an account of 'radical' or 'absolute' freedom"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: It is on bad faith
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre 4.2: "the chapter on bad faith in Being and Nothingness"

claims.claim: It is on 'the look' of others
claims.evidence: SEP Sartre 4.3: "his descriptions of being subject to the look of another"

items.fix: "One of the movement's defining books, alongside Beauvoir's work of the period, on ..."

claims.claim: The Second Sex is by Simone de Beauvoir, 1949
claims.evidence: SEP Beauvoir 1: "The Second Sex (1949)"; IEP e: "In 1949 Le Deuxième Sexe is published in France"

claims.claim: It shows how women are cast as man's 'Other', and man as the essential being
claims.evidence: SEP Beauvoir 7: "the claim central to the book: woman is the Other, man is the essential being"; quote verbatim; IEP e: "she becomes the other of man"

claims.claim: It is a founding text of second-wave feminism
claims.evidence: IEP e: "later a founding text of Second Wave Feminism"

claims.claim: Second-wave feminism = the women's movement of the 1960s and 1970s
claims.evidence: IEP e: "the feminist movement from the early 60's to the 70's"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: In Germany, critics such as Adorno called existentialism obscure, abstract and even mystical, Heidegger above all
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "In Germany, existentialism (and especially Heidegger) was criticised for being obscure, abstract or even mystical in nature. This criticism was made especially by Adorno"

claims.claim: Many other philosophers agreed
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "The criticism was echoed by many in the analytic tradition" (loses 'analytic' but stays true)

claims.claim: After Marxist criticism in the 1940s and 1950s, Sartre himself decided his early idea of 'radical' freedom was too abstract
claims.evidence: SEP 4.2: "in the wake of Marxist criticism in the 1940s and 1950s, his views changed; he realized that this early account was far too abstract"

claims.claim: Gloss: radical freedom = freedom made by choice alone
claims.evidence: SEP 4.2: "where we make or create ourselves ex nihilo, through the sheer 'upsurge' of choice alone"

claims.claim: It ignored the social conditions that limit real choices
claims.evidence: SEP 4.2: "It failed to engage the social, historical, and material conditions that invariably limit and constrain our freedom"

claims.claim: Merleau-Ponty was a French philosopher
claims.evidence: OpenStax Phenomenology and Reality: "French thinker Maurice Merleau-Ponty"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Merleau-Ponty objected that no one is free apart from other people and history
claims.evidence: IEP e: "Merleau-Ponty heavily criticizes the Sartrean stand"; "my freedom is interwoven with that of others by way of the world"; "the subjective free-will is always in a dialectical relationship with its historical context"

claims.claim: Later French thinkers faulted Sartre for neglecting language and the impersonal structures that shape meaning
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "In France, philosophers like Sartre were criticised by those newly under the influence of structuralism for paying insufficient attention to the nature of language and to impersonal structures of meaning"

claims.claim: Critics said existentialists neglected social and political structures, with dangerous results
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "Heidegger and the existentialist were also taken to task for paying insufficient attention to social and political structures or values, with dangerous results"

claims.claim: Heidegger is notorious for his involvement with the Nazis in the 1930s
claims.evidence: IEP c: "He remains notorious for his involvement with National Socialism in the 1930s"

claims.claim: Nietzsche's ideal of the self-creating individual is openly elitist and anti-democratic
claims.evidence: SEP 5.3: "the individual who can overcome ... for the sake of self-creation as an 'Overman'"; "his account of authenticity is unapologetically elitist and anti-democratic"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: The Nazis exploited his work, a use the IEP calls 'utterly misdirected'
claims.evidence: IEP b. Nietzsche: "The exploitation of his teaching by the Nazi ideologues ..., although utterly misdirected"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Camus accused Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger of escaping into 'forced hope'
claims.evidence: SEP Camus 3.3: "explicitly written against existentialists such as Shestov, Kierkegaard, Jaspers, and Heidegger"; "he rejects what he sees as their ultimate escapism"; "That forced hope is religious in all of them"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Gloss: forced hope = turning to God, or something beyond this life, to escape the absurd
claims.evidence: SEP Camus 3.3: "by seeking to appeal to something beyond the limits of the human condition, by turning to the transcendent"; Kierkegaard "seeks to be cured of it by making it an attribute of a God". 'God' is supported; 'beyond this life' reads as an afterlife, which the source does not say (it says beyond the limits of the human condition).

claims.claim: Some argue the label does more harm than good, lumping very different ideas together
claims.evidence: IEP intro: "insofar as it leads us ... to conflate together significantly different ideas – does more harm than good"; quote verbatim

items.fix: "He meant turning to God, or to something beyond the limits of the human condition, to escape the absurd."

claims.claim: Existentialism reached far beyond philosophy
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "how it stretched far beyond the literary and academic worlds"

claims.claim: Into films by Ingmar Bergman and Jean-Luc Godard
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "Its ideas are captured in films by Ingmar Bergman, Michelangelo Antonioni, Jean-Luc Godard"; IEP a: "Bergman and Godard are often associated with existentialist themes"

claims.claim: Into theatre, above all the plays of Beckett
claims.evidence: IEP a: "Within drama, the theatre of the absurd and most obviously Beckett were influenced by existentialist ideas"

claims.claim: Into painting, from Edvard Munch to Edward Hopper
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "Its moods are expressed in the paintings of Edvard Munch, ... and Edward Hopper"

claims.claim: Into the politics of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "informed the radical and emancipatory politics of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X"

claims.claim: Into the writing of Richard Wright and Ralph Ellison
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "the writings of Black intellectuals such as Ralph Ellison, Richard Wright"

claims.claim: Into feminism, through Beauvoir
claims.evidence: SEP 7.4: "Beauvoir's pioneering account ... in The Second Sex is well known for laying the conceptual foundations for second wave feminism"

claims.claim: Into Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks, on colonised Black people
claims.evidence: SEP 7.4: "her ideas would inform Franz Fanon's Black Skin, White Masks ..., a seminal work that disclosed the dehumanizing experience of colonized Black populations"

claims.claim: Into psychotherapy, in the work of Frankl, May and Yalom
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "a profound impact in the development of humanistic and existential approaches to psychotherapy in the work of ... Rollo May, Viktor Frankl, and Irvin Yalom"

claims.claim: Among philosophers, verdicts differ
claims.evidence: Framing of the IEP b. Philosophy vs SEP 7 contrast that follows; both cited

claims.claim: The IEP finds the movement as a whole has had relatively little direct influence within philosophy
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "As a whole, existentialism has had relatively little direct influence within philosophy"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Yet Nietzsche and Heidegger remain very much alive
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "Nietzsche and Heidegger in particular are very much 'live' topics in philosophy, even in the 21st century"

claims.claim: The IEP adds that the movement made emotion a serious subject of research
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "the philosophical importance that the existentialists placed upon emotion has been influential, legitimising a whole domain of philosophical research"

claims.claim: The movement insisted philosophy deal directly with real-life topics such as sex and death
claims.evidence: IEP b. Philosophy: "existentialism was a philosophy that insisted philosophy could and should deal very directly with 'real world' topics such as sex, death or crime"

claims.claim: The SEP sees the movement thriving
claims.evidence: SEP 7: "the movement continues to thrive in the academy today"

claims.claim: Its courses are among philosophy's most popular
claims.evidence: SEP 7.7: "Existentialist-themed courses are often among the most popular in the philosophy curriculum". The hedge 'often' is dropped, so a frequent pattern becomes a flat fact.

claims.claim: It shaped later French thinkers such as Foucault and Derrida
claims.evidence: SEP 7.1: "a decisive impact on post-structural philosophies in France. Nietzsche and Heidegger in particular served as decisive influences on ... Jacques Derrida's method of deconstruction and in Michel Foucault's genealogy of power"

claims.claim: It shaped theories of the self as a life story
claims.evidence: SEP 7.2: "existentialism has also informed key developments in narrative and hermeneutic philosophy"; "this conception of narrative identity"

claims.claim: It shaped the science of the mind, which now sees the mind as rooted in the body
claims.evidence: SEP 7.3: "philosophers of mind and cognitive scientists have been drawing on existentialist philosophy"; "replaced the picture of the disembodied mind with the now widely accepted notion of the embedded, enactive, and embodied self"

claims.claim: It shaped medicine and nursing
claims.evidence: SEP 7.6: "we have seen its influence emerge in a range of different areas, from narrative medicine to nursing"

items.fix: "... and its courses are often among philosophy's most popular."

claims.claim: Existentialism is a loose movement
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "one finds secular and religious existentialists, philosophers who embrace a conception of radical freedom and others who reject it" (the word 'loose' itself is in IEP intro, not cited here; meaning supported)

claims.claim: It begins from real, lived human life
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "The human condition is revealed through an examination of the ways we concretely engage with the world in our everyday lives"

claims.claim: It is rooted in Kierkegaard and Nietzsche
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "the conceptual groundwork of the movement was laid much earlier in the nineteenth century by pioneers like Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche"

claims.claim: It was made famous by Sartre and Beauvoir in mid-20th-century France
claims.evidence: SEP intro: "an intellectual movement that exploded on the scene in mid-twentieth-century France"; "the most popular voices of this movement were French, most notably Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir"

claims.claim: Camus rejected the label
claims.evidence: SEP Camus 1: "Camus denied being an existentialist"

claims.claim: Heidegger rejected the label
claims.evidence: IEP c: "he repudiates any possible connection of his philosophy with the existentialism of Sartre"; "Heidegger's own repudiation of existentialism"

claims.claim: Theme: existence before essence
claims.evidence: SEP 3. Existence Precedes Essence (section title and content)

claims.claim: Theme: freedom and anxiety
claims.evidence: SEP 4.1 The Anxiety of Choice

claims.claim: Theme: authenticity versus the crowd
claims.evidence: SEP 5: "Rather than living our own lives, we tend to get pulled along by the crowd, doing what 'they' do"

claims.claim: Theme: meaning without guarantees
claims.evidence: SEP 1: "there is no overarching reason, order, or purpose to our existence"

claims.claim: Theme: my freedom needs yours
claims.evidence: SEP 6: "My freedom, then, is not free-floating; it is invariably bound up in the freedom of others"

claims.claim: Theme: faith and the leap
claims.evidence: SEP 5.2: "Abraham becomes a 'knight of faith' by 'leaping' (springer) into a paradox"

claims.claim: Existentialists do not look at life from a cool distance
claims.evidence: SEP 2: "we cannot look down on the human condition from a detached, third-person perspective"

claims.claim: They start from a person caught up in living
claims.evidence: SEP 2: "a philosophy that begins from the standpoint of the engagé, of the individual who is engaged in life"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Kierkegaard wanted 'a truth which is true for me'
claims.evidence: SEP 2.1: "it discloses 'a truth which is true for me'"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Gloss: lived and felt rather than just known
claims.evidence: SEP 2.1: "to live this truth"; "It is an ineffable truth that is felt rather than known"

claims.claim: Their ideas shaped existential psychotherapy
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Objective: "interventions that draw on themes from existential philosophy"; IEP a: "a more explicit taking up of existentialist themes is found in the broad 'existentialist psychotherapy' movement"

claims.claim: Gloss: it helps people with questions such as meaning and the fear of death
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Objective: "to help clients address such issues in their lives as meaning and death anxiety"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Logotherapy is one example
claims.evidence: IEP a lists "the Austrian Frankl, who invented the method of logotherapy" among existentialist psychotherapy figures

claims.claim: Gloss: logotherapy is a therapy built around finding meaning
claims.evidence: VFI Vienna: "meaning-centered approach to psychotherapy"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Invented by the Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl
claims.evidence: IEP a: "the Austrian Frankl, who invented the method of logotherapy"; quote verbatim; VFI Vienna: "the psychiatrist and neurologist Viktor Emil Frankl"

claims.claim: For existentialists, no god and no absolute moral law can guide our choices or justify them
claims.evidence: SEP 4: "There is no moral absolute, divine will, or natural law that can provide guidance or justify our actions"

claims.claim: We alone are responsible, and realising that often brings anxiety
claims.evidence: SEP 4: "the awareness is often accompanied by anxiety because we realize that we alone are responsible for our choices"

claims.claim: Sartre: 'there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us'
claims.evidence: SEP 4: "'there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us' (Sartre 1946 [2001, 296])"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Sartre's own example is a student of his in wartime France
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "the case of a pupil of mine"; "inclined to be a 'collaborator'"; "the German offensive of 1940"

claims.claim: The student's brother had been killed in the German attack of 1940
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "his elder brother had been killed in the German offensive of 1940"

claims.claim: He could go to England and fight with the Free French Forces, or stay with his mother
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "the choice between going to England to join the Free French Forces or of staying near his mother"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: His mother lived only for him
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "He fully realised that this woman lived only for him"

claims.claim: He came to Sartre for advice
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "the youth did, at least, go to a professor to ask for advice"; "in coming to me"

claims.claim: Choosing an adviser is already a choice
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "to choose an adviser is nevertheless to commit oneself by that choice"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: You more or less know what they will say
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "at bottom you already knew, more or less, what he would advise"

claims.claim: His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.'
claims.evidence: Sartre EIH: "I had but one reply to make. You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent."; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Application is labelled as ours: 'One way to use his point: ...'
claims.evidence: Label present; the self-question is framed as our use, not Sartre's instruction

claims.claim: For Sartre and Beauvoir, no fixed meaning is handed to us
claims.evidence: SEP 5.5: "My projects have meaning and value because I chose these projects, but the meaning is contingent; it is never enduring or stable"

claims.claim: Beauvoir said existence is not absurd but ambiguous: 'its meaning is never fixed'
claims.evidence: SEP 5.5: "The notion of ambiguity must not be confused with that of absurdity ... to say that it is ambiguous is to assert that its meaning is never fixed"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: A 2015 review pooled the results of 15 trials of existential therapies
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Results: "Twenty-one eligible randomized controlled trials ... from which 15 studies with unique data were included"; quote verbatim; Method: "Weighted pooled mean effects were calculated"

claims.claim: Meaning-focused therapies had large effects on people's sense of meaning
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Results: "Meaning therapies (n = 6 studies) showed large effects on positive meaning in life"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: It found most support for structured programmes that discussed meaning directly with physically ill patients
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Conclusion: "We found particular support for structured interventions incorporating psychoeducation, exercises, and discussing meaning in life directly and positively with physically ill patients"; quote verbatim ('most' for 'particular' is borderline but acceptable)

claims.claim: The studies were few and low in quality
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Conclusion: "Despite the small number and low quality of studies"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: That is evidence for therapy, not for reflecting alone (guardrail: meta-analysis not presented as evidence for the self-exercise)
claims.evidence: Vos 2015 Objective/Method: the review covers therapies, "psychological interventions"; the text explicitly scopes it away from self-reflection. Guardrail passes.

claims.claim: Frankl held that we discover meaning rather than make it
claims.evidence: VFIL Meaning: "Frankl maintained that meaning exists for us to discover"; quote verbatim; "we can discover meaning but we can't make meaning"

claims.claim: We should not ask what life means, but recognise 'that it is he who is asked'
claims.evidence: VFIL Life has ultimate meaning: "man should not ask what the meaning of his life is, but rather must recognize that it is he who is asked"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Logotherapists often use Socratic dialogue in therapy
claims.evidence: VFI Vienna Socratic dialogue: "Socratic dialogue is a conversational method frequently used by logotherapists"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Gloss: Socratic dialogue = guiding a person by asking questions
claims.evidence: VFI Vienna Socratic dialogue: "this technique of guiding by questioning was introduced by Socrates"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: They help clients find meanings for themselves
claims.evidence: VFI Vienna Will to Meaning: "they are not offered specific meanings. Rather, they are guided and assisted in the realization of those meaning possibilities they have detected themselves"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: The Viktor Frankl Institute of Logotherapy names three avenues to meaning
claims.evidence: VFIL Three avenues: "He called these the creative, experiential and attitudinal avenues to meaning-discovery"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Avenue 1: what you gave, through work or deeds
claims.evidence: VFIL: "Creative actions. Giving of ourselves and contributing to life through meaningful work, deeds"

claims.claim: Avenue 2: what you received, through experiences or relationships
claims.evidence: VFIL: "Experiences. Receiving from life through meaningful experiences or relationships"

claims.claim: Avenue 3: the stance you took, especially towards suffering you could not avoid
claims.evidence: VFIL: "Attitudes. Adopting the right attitude to situations, especially those of unavoidable suffering"

claims.claim: Application is labelled as ours: 'One way to borrow that on your own: ...'
claims.evidence: Label present; self-use is not claimed as logotherapy practice and no evidence is attached to it

claims.claim: For Nietzsche, the key to giving your life its own style is radical acceptance
claims.evidence: SEP 5.3: "The key to living with style is, for Nietzsche, a radical acceptance"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Gloss: radical acceptance = saying yes to your whole life, the good and the bad
claims.evidence: SEP 5.3: "a radical acceptance of one's existence and the world as it is, embracing all our strengths and weaknesses and all the blessed and cursed events"

claims.claim: He called this attitude amor fati: love of one's fate
claims.evidence: SEP 5.3: "overflowing with amor fati (love of one's fate), the Overman welcomes this possibility"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: Only 'the highest types' have that kind of freedom
claims.evidence: SEP 5.3: "For Nietzsche, only 'the highest types' can manifest this kind of freedom and capacity for self-overcoming"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: A demon tells you that you must live this life again, 'innumerable times', with nothing new in it
claims.evidence: Joyful Wisdom §341: "thou must live it once more, and also innumerable times; and there will be nothing new in it"

claims.claim: Would you curse the demon?
claims.evidence: §341: "curse the demon that so spake?"

claims.claim: Or answer that you never heard anything more divine?
claims.evidence: §341: "Thou art a God, and never did I hear aught more divine!"

claims.claim: If the thought took hold of you, it would transform you, or perhaps crush you
claims.evidence: §341: "If that thought acquired power over thee, as thou art, it would transform thee, and perhaps crush thee"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: The question 'Dost thou want this once more, and also for innumerable times?' would lie as the heaviest burden on everything you do
claims.evidence: §341: "the question with regard to all and everything: 'Dost thou want this once more, and also for innumerable times?' would lie as the heaviest burden upon thy activity!" (inline quote verbatim)

claims.claim: One influential reading treats it as a test of whether your life has been good
claims.evidence: SEP Nietzsche 6.3: "an influential line of readings has argued ... a practical thought experiment designed to test whether one's life has been good"; quote verbatim

claims.claim: He meant your life as a whole, in every detail
claims.evidence: §341: "every pain and every joy and every thought and every sigh, and all the unspeakably small and great in thy life"; SEP 6.3: "what recurs is the same in every detail"; "our life as a whole"
